CausalChain: Liver injury → increased ROS → accumulation of p62 due to oxidative stress and impaired autophagy → p62 competitively binds Keap1 reducing its inhibition of Nrf2 → sustained Nrf2 activation leads to upregulation of cytoprotective genes but also promotes metabolic shifts that can activate hepatic stellate cells and support tumor cell survival → periodic activation of autophagy clears p62, resetting the Nrf2 response → controlled, intermittent Nrf2 activation produces cytoprotection without promoting fibrosis or oncogenesis
Hypothesis: Targeted intermittent induction of selective autophagy combined with controlled pharmacological activation of Nrf2 can create a balanced therapeutic window in liver diseases, providing protection against oxidative injury while preventing pro-fibrotic and tumorigenic consequences of sustained Nrf2 activation.
Abstract: The Nrf2 pathway plays a critical role in defending liver cells against oxidative stress by inducing a range of antioxidant and cytoprotective genes. However, sustained activation of Nrf2, partly mediated by persistent p62 accumulation due to impaired autophagy, may inadvertently foster a cellular environment that promotes metabolic reprogramming, hepatic stellate cell activation, and even tumorigenesis. In this context, fine‐tuning the autophagy–Nrf2 axis could offer a strategy to achieve short‐term cytoprotection without the long‐term risk of fibrosis and liver cancer. Here we propose that a therapeutic regimen combining intermittent induction of selective autophagy with controlled modulation of Nrf2 activation might harness the antioxidant benefits of the pathway while limiting its oncogenic potential.
